passages.title: The Evolution of Publishing in a Digital Era
passages.text:
The Internet makes possible the instantaneous transmission and retrieval of digital text. It is widely assumed that this capacity will lead to the displacement of printed books by digitized books that are read mainly on computer screens or handheld electronic devices. But it is more likely, I believe, that most digital files of books will be printed and bound on demand at point of sale by machines that can quickly and inexpensively make single copies that are indistinguishable from books made in factories. Once most books have been digitized, anyone with access to the Internet will be able to purchase printed books from a practically limitless digital catalog that includes even those books that, under traditional publishing assumptions, would have been designated “out of print.”

Also, the digital publication of a book online involves no physical inventory, thereby eliminating the costs of warehousing, shipping books to wholesalers and to retail stores, displaying physical books in retail stores, and returning unsold books to publishers. This would make digital publishing much less expensive than traditional publishing. Given the economic efficiency and convenience for customers of this new digital model of publishing, it is likely to eventually supplant or at least rival traditional publishing—although it will be some time before a catalog of printable digitized books becomes large enough to justify investment in book printing machines at numerous regional sites.

Moreover, the elimination of whole categories of expense means that under the digital publishing model, authors would be responsible for a greater proportion of the value of the final product and would therefore, according to literary agents, be entitled to a larger share of the proceeds. Currently a large percentage of publishers’ revenue is absorbed by the costs of printing, selling, and distributing physical books, costs that are irrelevant to digital publication. Literary agents marketing new manuscripts could thus be expected to demand a significantly bigger slice of revenue for their authors than has been traditional. But large, established publishing houses, which are heavily invested in the infrastructure of traditional publishing, initially will be reluctant to accede. So the opportunity to bid for new manuscripts will go first to upstart digital-publishing firms unfettered by traditional practices or infrastructure. Under this competitive pressure, traditional publishers will have to reduce their redundant functions in order to accommodate higher royalty payments to authors or else they will lose their authors. Such adjustments are typical of the interval between a departing economic model and its successor and may help explain the caution with which today’s publishing conglomerates are approaching the digital future.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

How digital publishing will transform the publishing business — and create competitive pressure to pay authors a larger share of revenue.

**Framework**

Highlight Noteworthy / Predictive Argument. The author argues for a particular vision of digital publishing's future and its economic consequences for authors.

**Main Point**

Digital publishing will transform the economics of the publishing business — and the resulting shift in costs will create competitive pressure to pay authors a significantly greater share of revenue, with upstart digital publishers leading the way.

**P1: A different prediction about digital publishing**

It's widely assumed that printed books will be displaced by digitized books read on screens. The author thinks instead that most digital files will be printed and bound on demand at point of sale. With digitization, anyone with internet access can purchase from a practically limitless catalog — including books that would have been "out of print."

**P2: Digital publishing eliminates whole categories of cost**

No physical inventory means no warehousing, no shipping to wholesalers/retailers, no in-store display, no unsold-book returns. Much less expensive than traditional publishing. Digital publishing is likely to supplant or rival traditional publishing — though it'll take time to build out the catalog and printing infrastructure.

**P3: Authors should get a bigger share — and competitive pressure will deliver it**

With whole categories of expense eliminated, authors are responsible for a greater proportion of the value of the final product, so (literary agents say) they're entitled to a larger share. Currently a large percentage of publisher revenue is absorbed by costs irrelevant to digital publication. Agents will demand bigger slices for authors. Established publishers, invested in old infrastructure, will be reluctant. The opportunity to bid for new manuscripts will go first to upstart digital firms unfettered by old practices. Under that competitive pressure, traditional publishers will have to reduce redundant functions and accommodate higher royalties — or lose authors. This explains the publishing conglomerates' caution toward the digital future.
summaries.brief:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

Digital publishing's transformation of the industry and its impact on author royalties.

**Framework**

Predictive Argument.

**Main Point**

Digital publishing will transform the economics of publishing and create competitive pressure to pay authors more.

**P1: The author's prediction**

Most digital files will be printed on demand at point of sale, not just read on screens.

**P2: Cost savings**

Digital publishing eliminates warehousing, shipping, retail display, and returns.

**P3: Author royalties will rise**

Authors are entitled to a larger share; upstart digital firms will outbid traditional publishers, forcing them to raise royalties.
summaries.anotherWay:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The author is making a prediction about how digital publishing will reshape the book business — and especially how it'll change what authors get paid.

**Framework**

Predictive Argument.

**Main Point**

The simpler version: most people think digital publishing means everyone reads on screens. The author thinks the bigger story is print-on-demand — physical books printed when ordered, with no warehouse and no shipping costs. That kills off huge chunks of what publishing currently spends money on. Once those costs are gone, authors deserve and will demand a bigger cut. Upstart digital publishers will lead the way; traditional publishers will be forced to follow or lose their authors.

**P1: The contrarian prediction**

Most assume digital = screens. The author predicts: most digital files will get printed on demand at the store, indistinguishable from factory-made books, with limitless catalog including "out of print" titles.

**P2: The cost story**

Digital publishing eliminates warehouses, wholesale shipping, retail shipping, in-store display, and unsold-book returns. That's a huge chunk of traditional publishing cost.

**P3: How that hits authors**

If those costs are gone, the publisher is doing less work for the value of the final book. So authors deserve more. Agents will push for bigger royalty shares. Big publishers will resist — they have all that old infrastructure to defend. So upstart digital firms will outbid them for new manuscripts. To keep their authors, traditional publishers will have to cut redundant work and pay higher royalties.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements most accurately expresses the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Do we have a most valuable sentence? If so, that can serve as our prephrase.

It would seem like the 3rd sentence of the passage is the main point. We had an attribution in the 2nd sentence: "it is widely assumed that printed books will disappear and we'll read book on screens".

And then the author gives us the signature Challenge Position *Pivot + Pushback* in the 3rd sentence: "No, it's more likely that people will print a digitized book on demand by a machine that make a single hard copy of book."

The rest of the passage fleshes out this prediction. P2 begins with "Also" and P3 begins with "Moreover", each of which signal that this paragraph is just adding supporting points to some bigger idea that already happened.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for an answer saying something like, "The future of the book publishing industry is gonna mainly be printing a hard copy of a book on demand from a point of sale machine."

choices.text: The shift from traditional to digital publishing is typical of the shift from one economic model to a more efficient economic model.
choices.explanation:
This casts the passage as a *Theme / Example* type passage, where the transformation happening in the book industry is only being discussed to illuminate this broader theme.

But this passage doesn't start with a broader theme and then zoom in to the book example. It starts right away by discussing the publishing industry. That is the central topic. The main point should be about the publishing industry.

The author's main thought about the industry isn't that, "They're undergoing a shift that is similar to other industries who shift models". It's more like, "They're shifting from mass printing books ahead of time, storing them in a warehouse, shipping them to retail stores, etc. .... to digitizing all of them and letting people print one copy of any book they want at a print-a-book kiosk."

choices.text: Digital publishing is likely to one day rival traditional publishing, but social and economic factors are currently hindering its acceptance.
choices.explanation:
The passage argues that digital publishing will transform the industry and is likely to supplant or rival traditional publishing. The time delay is based on "having a catalog of printable digitized books large enough to justify investment in book printing machines at numerous sites".

The author never says its ascension is being slowed down by social and economic factors. In P3 we briefly mention that large publishing houses will be reluctant to give authors a bigger slice of revenues, but the author doesn't portray that as hindering the acceptance of digital publishing.

She just says it will create an opportunity for upstart digital firms to swoop in.

choices.text: Digital publishing will be convenient for readers and profitable for publishers but will also result in a great deal of movement by authors among different publishing houses.
choices.tag: Too Strong (will result in great movement)
choices.explanation:
There's too much emphasis here on an idea that the author doesn't really say. P3 alludes to a possible tension between authors who want a bigger slice of the revenue pie and large publishing houses who don't want to give it to them. And she indicates that these authors might be swayed to sign instead with upstart digital firms. But she doesn't guarantee that there will be a great of movement.

She portrays it more as a situation where large publishing houses will be forced to get over their initial reluctance because they realize that *otherwise* they might lose a great deal of authors to newer firms.

choices.text: Although digital books can now be displayed on computers and handheld electronic devices, consumers will demonstrate that they prefer books printed at the point of sale.
choices.explanation:
It's never actually established that digital books can *currently* be displayed on computers and handheld devices. This is a prediction of things to come. The author does predict that printing books at point of sale will be the dominant model and does think that it will have advantages for consumers, but she never actually guarantees that consumers **will demonstrate** that they prefer books printed at point of sale.

Plus, this answer would only wrap its arms around P1. The passage also discussed how this new business model would affect publishers and authors, and this answer would be capturing none of that P2 or P3 discussion.

choices.text: Digital publishing will transform the economics of the publishing business and in doing so will likely create competitive pressures to pay authors a greater percentage of publishers' net revenue.
choices.explanation: Paragraph 2 explains cost reductions and paragraph 3 traces their consequences for agents demands, new competitors and traditional publishers. This answer captures that broader economic argument. Print on demand is the proposed mechanism, while the pressure for higher author shares is a major consequence developed across the passage.

questions.prompt: The author uses the phrase "whole categories of expense" (first sentence of the third paragraph) primarily to refer to

choices.text: the fees collected by literary agents from their clients
choices.explanation: Literary agents are expected to remain under the digital publishing model (third paragraph).

choices.text: the price paid to have books printed and bound
choices.explanation: Printing and binding books would continue under the digital publishing model (first paragraph).

choices.text: the royalties paid to authors by their publishers
choices.explanation: The royalties paid to authors are expected to increase under the digital publishing model (third paragraph).

choices.text: the costs specific to the retail trade in traditional printed books
choices.explanation: The categories of expense refer to printing, selling, and distributing books (third paragraph) which are costs specific to the retail trade.

choices.text: the total sales of a book minus the value of those books returned unsold to the bookseller
choices.explanation: The total sales of a book cannot be a category of expense. Sales and expenses are on opposite sides of an accounting ledger.

questions.prompt: It can most reasonably be inferred that the author would agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.text: Those publishers that fail to embrace the new digital model of publishing will be unlikely to remain economically competitive.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the second paragraph.

choices.text: The primary threat to the spread of digital publishing will be the widespread use of computers and handheld devices for reading text.
choices.explanation: Threats to the spread of digital publishing are not discussed in the passage.

choices.text: Any book will sell more copies if it is published digitally than if it is published traditionally.
choices.explanation: The passage does not indicate whether a book will sell more copies in the digital or traditional publishing models.

choices.text: Digital publishing will allow publishers to substantially decrease the amount of money they allocate for advertising their books.
choices.explanation: Advertising is not listed as a category of expense likely to have a reduction in cost.

choices.explanation: This is supported in the second paragraph.

choices.explanation: Books in the digital publishing model will still need their book covers designed.

choices.explanation: This is supported in the second paragraph.

choices.explanation: This is supported in line 20.

choices.explanation: This is supported in the second paragraph.

questions.prompt: If the scenario described in the first two paragraphs were to become true, then which one of the following would most likely be the case?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Let's remind ourselves what the "scenario described in the first two paragraphs" was: the author is talking about an end to one business model and the beginning of a new one.

OLD:
Someone writes a book. A publisher decides to print 10,000 copies of it and distribute it to book stores. The book stores sometimes sell out of copies and request more, so the publisher gets them some of the spare copies being kept in a warehouse somewhere. The book stores sometimes fail to sell the copies and return those unsold books to publishers (do the book stores get a partial refund?)

NEW:
Someone writes a book. A publisher digitizes it. A person can then either download an electronic copy of the book onto a handheld electronic device (like a Kindle / iPad), or he person goes to one of these book printing kiosks and says, "I'd like a copy of *How the LSAT Can Make You a Better Person*", and then waits a few minutes while the book printing kiosk prints a single copy of the book, that the customer then walks away with.

It's really hard to predict where the answers might go from here, because there's a lot to that scenario. Let's be cautious about strong language and find the most supportable answer we can.

choices.text: The need for warehousing will shift mainly from that of individual books to that of paper and binding material to make books.
choices.explanation:
This is supported in the first and second paragraphs.

It is a weirdly "common sense" supported answer. There's no great line reference. We definitely never talk about "binding material". But it comports with the sense that publishers will no longer be pre-printing tons of copies of a book and stashing those in a warehouse.

Instead, they will be creating these self-serve kiosks that print a book on demand. Those kiosks will need paper and binding material if they're going to print someone a book on demand, and so the kiosks will need to be periodically replenished with more paper and binding supplies, and so the people who manage those kiosks (presumably the publishers) will probably have a big supply room of paper and binding material so that when a technician goes out to re-supply the kiosk, they will have materials with which to supply it.

choices.text: The patronage of stores that sell used books will increase significantly.
choices.explanation: Used books are not discussed in the passage.

choices.text: Most publishers will sell their own books individually and will not use distributors or retailers.
choices.explanation: While publishers will not use distributors (third paragraph), they may still use retailers.

choices.text: There will be significantly less demand by publishers for the services of copy editors and book designers.
choices.explanation: The passage identifies savings in physical inventory, distribution and retail display, but does not predict a reduction in demand for copy editing or design. Absence of that prediction does not establish that demand will remain exactly the same.

choices.text: The demand for book-grade paper will decrease significantly.
choices.explanation: The demand for book-grade paper is not discussed in the passage.

choices.text: The changing literary tastes of consumers will be the main cause of the eventual transition to the new digital model.

choices.text: The ease of keeping books "in print" will be the primary factor in the eventual acceptance of the new digital model.
choices.explanation: The economics of digital publishing will be the main impetus to the new model (second paragraph).

choices.text: The demands of literary agents will be the impetus for completing the transition to the new digital model.
choices.explanation: This is supported in the third paragraph.

choices.text: The development of innovative marketing strategies will ensure acceptance of the new digital model.
choices.explanation: The economics of digital publishing will be the main impetus to the new model (second paragraph).

choices.text: Widespread familiarity with new ways of storing information will be the primary reason for the acceptance of the new digital model.
choices.explanation: The economics of digital publishing will be the main impetus to the new model (second paragraph).

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the final sentence of the passage is to

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
When we're asked about the purpose of a sentence/detail, we try to remind ourselves of the context in the sentence or two leading up to it.

Overall this final paragraph is saying that in this new digital publishing world, authors will start asking for a bigger cut of book revenue (since the publisher no longer needs to pay for thinks like printing / storing / shipping physical books).

Then the paragraph ends with a contrast between older/larger publishers who will resist this change and younger/nimbler publishers who will be embracing the digital model.

The final sentence begins with a pronoun, "**Such** adjustments ...", so we know it's elaborating on whatever adjustments were described in the preceding sentence.

The preceding sentence was saying that these older/larger publishers are going to have to **adjust** their ways and be willing to give authors a bigger cut of money, or else the authors will go to the newer publishers.

The final sentence essentially is saying that the way the book publishing business model is shifting will follow a typical economic pattern and saying these older, established companies are not looking forward to this.

choices.text: suggest that traditional publishing houses have been too slow to embrace digital publishing
choices.tag: Out of Scope: have been too slow
choices.explanation: The final sentence explicitly refers to todays publishers caution, but explains it through a familiar economic transition. It does not judge that they have been too slow. Explanation of caution is different from criticism of delay.

choices.text: provide a broader context that helps to clarify the situation facing traditional publishers
choices.explanation:
The last sentence does connect the situation the traditional publishers are going through to a broader economic pattern:

*Such adjustments (as the ones that traditional publishers are going through) are **typical** of the interval between a departing model and its successor*.

The author is saying, "The story I just told you about digital publishing is similar to other stories I could tell you about other industries when an old model gets replaced by a new model."

choices.text: summarize the argument for the claim that digital publishing will likely replace traditional publishing
choices.explanation: The final sentence places the anticipated adjustments in a broader economic pattern and suggests an explanation for current caution. It does not recapitulate the preceding cost-efficiency and competition case. Whether a sentence can itself contain an argument is not what makes this option wrong.

choices.text: illustrate the primary obstacle facing traditional publishing houses that wish to incorporate digital publishing capabilities
choices.explanation:
The last sentence doesn't mention any obstacle that a traditional publishing house would face as they attempt to go digital.

A few sentences prior, we hear that one "obstacle" in going digital would be agreeing to let authors take a bigger cut of the book revenue.

This sentence doesn't provide any illustration of that (e.g. "previously the author only got 40% of net revenue, but now they're likely to demand upwards of 65%.")

choices.text: recommend a wait-and-see approach on the part of traditional publishing houses
choices.explanation: The final sentence is not a recommendation. It just describes a situation as typical of a broader economic pattern reiterates the causal reason why big publishing houses are nervous.

passages.title: Reliability and Admissibility of Fingerprint Evidence
passages.text:
**Passage A**

In this appeal of his criminal conviction, the defendant challenges the fingerprint evidence used against him at trial, claiming that fingerprint identification theory has not been adequately tested. He cites the inability of the fingerprint examiner who incriminated him at trial to name any studies establishing that no two persons have identical fingerprints.

The defendant claims that there are no established error rates revealing how often fingerprint examiners incorrectly identify a fingerprint as a particular person’s, and asserts that fingerprint examiners lack uniform, objective standards. He cites testimony given by the fingerprint examiner at trial that there is no generally accepted standard regarding the number of “points of identification” required for a positive identification.

Although fingerprint identification has not attained the status of scientific law, it has been used in criminal trials for 100 years, and experts have long concurred about its reliability. While further testing and the development of even more consistent standards may be desirable, this court sees no reason to reject outright a form of evidence that has so ably withstood the test of time.

While it may be true that different agencies require different degrees of correlation before permitting a positive identification, fingerprint examiners are held to a consistent “points and characteristics” approach to identification. As the fingerprint expert testified at the defendant’s trial, examiners are regularly subjected to testing and proficiency requirements, and uniform standards have been established through professional training and peer review. The trial court below was therefore within its discretion in crediting testimony that fingerprint identification has an exceedingly low error rate.

**Passage B**

Fingerprint examiners lack objective standards for evaluating whether two prints “match.” There is simply no consensus about what constitutes a sufficient basis for identification. Some examiners use a “point-counting” method that entails counting the number of similar “ridge” characteristics on prints, but there is no fixed requirement about how many points of similarity are needed, and local practices vary. Others reject point counting for a more holistic approach. Either way, there is no generally agreed-on standard for determining precisely when to declare a match.

Although we know that different individuals can share certain ridge characteristics, the chance of two individuals sharing any given number of identifying characteristics is unknown. How likely is it that two people could have four points of resemblance, or five, or eight? Moreover, fingerprints used in forensic identification are typically partial and smudged. Are the odds that two partial prints from different people will match one in a thousand, one in a million, or one in a billion? No fingerprint examiner can answer such questions decisively, yet the answers are critical to evaluating the value of fingerprint evidence.

The error rate for fingerprint identification in actual practice has received little systematic study. How often do fingerprint examiners mistakenly declare a match? Although some proficiency tests show examiners making few or no errors, these tests have been criticized as lax; a more rigorous test showed a 34 percent rate of erroneous identification.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The reliability and standards of fingerprint identification as evidence in criminal trials

**Framework**

Present Debate

**Main Point**

Passage A argues that while fingerprint identification may lack uniform scientific standards, it is a valuable and reliable form of evidence that courts should continue to accept. Passage B, in contrast, points out the lack of objective standards and the unknown error rates, challenging the premise that fingerprint identification is as reliable as claimed. *The Most Valuable Sentences:* - Passage A: “this court sees no reason to reject outright a form of evidence that has so ably withstood the test of time” (P3). - Passage B: “there is no generally agreed-on standard for determining precisely when to declare a match” (P1).

**Passage A: Court Response to the Challenge**

The defendant in a criminal trial challenges the fingerprint evidence used to convict him, focusing on the lack of scientific testing, absence of studies proving the uniqueness of fingerprints, and undefined error rates. He also criticizes the lack of uniform standards among examiners, especially regarding the number of matching features needed for identification.

**P2: Concerns About Standards and Error Rates**

The defendant argues that examiners don’t have consistent guidelines and references courtroom testimony that there's no standard for “points of identification.” He emphasizes that error rates for fingerprint misidentification aren't established.

**P3: Court Defense of Fingerprint Evidence**

Although the court concedes that fingerprint evidence isn’t a “scientific law,” it notes a long history of expert agreement on its reliability and widespread courtroom use. The judge acknowledges that more rigorous standards may be helpful, but sees no cause to reject print evidence entirely due to its track record.

**P4: Clarification of Current Standards and Error Rates**

The court further explains that, despite differences between agencies, fingerprint analysis relies on training, proficiency testing, and peer review, The court therefore accepts the trial court’s decision to credit testimony that the error rate is exceedingly low.

**Passage B: Critique of Fingerprint Identification**

B criticizes fingerprint identification methods, arguing there’s no objective, universally agreed standard for declaring a “match.” Practices differ between agencies; some count matching points while others use holistic methods, with no consensus on required similarity.

**P2: Uncertainty About Uniqueness and Probability**

The passage notes that no one knows the practical odds of matching fingerprints. Since prints collected in investigations are often partial or smudged, there’s no definitive answer about how likely it is to find matches between different people, highlighting a major limitation for evidence evaluation.

**P3: Error Rates and Testing Concerns**

B points out that actual error rates for fingerprint identification are largely unstudied in real-world settings. While some tests show few mistakes, they may not be strict enough, and at least one tough test found a 34% error rate, casting doubt on the method’s reliability.

**Summary Comments**

- The two passages present opposite views on the issue: Passage A defends fingerprint evidence, stressing tradition and expert consensus, while Passage B criticizes it for a lack of scientific rigor, objective standards, and clear error rates. - When confronted with scientific evidence in court, it’s common to see debates like this: one side emphasizes reliability and practicality, the other presses for methodological consistency and proof. - Both passages are helpful examples for questions that ask for the author’s attitude or request you to identify flaws or gaps in the opposing argument’s reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately expresses the main point of passage B?

choices.text: Criminal defendants do not always have a full and fair opportunity to challenge faulty fingerprint evidence when it is used against them at trial.
Fingerprint evidence has been shown to be too unreliable for use in criminal trials.
The error rate for fingerprint identification is significantly higher than is generally acknowledged.
There are a number of fundamental problems in the field of fingerprint identification as it is currently practiced.
There is a growing consensus within the legal community that fingerprint evidence is often unreliable.

questions.prompt: The authors would be most likely to disagree about

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
On a very basic level, we know that the author of A was more trusting of fingerprint evidence, as she upholds the use of it in the trial court proceedings. She says:
- examiners are held to a consistent approach
- examiners are regularly tested for proficiency
- uniform standards have been established
- fingerprinting has an exceedingly low error rate.

Meanwhile, the author of B was much more skeptical about how trustworthy fingerprinting is:
- fingerprint examiners ****lack**** uniform standards
- there is ****no**** consensus, no fixed requirement, no generally agreed-on standard
- error rate is unknown and may be as high as 34%

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: There are several possibilities there where the two mismatched, so we'll have to see what the answers are offering.

choices.text: whether uniformity in the training of fingerprint examiners is desirable
choices.explanation: Passage A emphasizes uniform standards as a good thing, and Passage B mentions a lack of uniformity as a bad thing, so they would both agree that we'd ****want**** uniform standards in training.

choices.text: the likelihood that a fingerprint examiner will incorrectly declare a match in a given criminal case
choices.explanation:
They definitely disagree in their assessment of the error rate of fingerprinting, with Passage A acting like *it's known that it's exceedingly low* and Passage B acting like *it's unknown / it's received little study.*

The final sentence of Passage A:
*the trial court was within its discretion in crediting testimony that fingerprint identification has an exceedingly low error rate.*

Final paragraph of Passage B:
*The error rate has received little systematic study ... a more rigorous test showed a 34% rate of error.*

This answer is somewhat frustrating because it's not like Passage A offers one number and Passage B offers a different number. But "exceedingly low" vs. "unknown / possibly as bad as 34%" are still two very different answers if someone is asked, "What's the likelihood a fingerprint examiner will incorrectly declare a match?"

choices.text: whether fingerprint identification should be accorded the status of scientific law
choices.explanation: A expressly concedes in paragraph 3 that fingerprint identification has not attained the status of scientific law. B questions its standards and evidentiary basis. Neither passage supplies support for a disagreement about whether it should be accorded that status.

choices.text: the relative merits of the point-counting and holistic methods of fingerprint identification
choices.explanation:
This answer is suggesting that one of the authors thinks that the point-counting system is better, while the other author thinks that the holistic method is better.

Neither author expressed a definitive preference one way or the other.

choices.text: whether different agencies vary in the degree of correlation they require for examiners to declare a match
choices.explanation:
It seems like both authors would agree that, yes, different agencies vary in the degree of correlation required of "a match".

The first sentence of Passage A's last paragraph says:
*While it may be true that different agencies require difference degrees of correlation ...*

And since Passage B thinks there aren't consistent standards anywhere, he would be likely to agree with that. His very first sentence suggests as much.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred that the author of passage A is

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The question stem is entirely unhelpful, so we'd consider this an *Undefined Target* and head to the answers.

If we scan the answers for a sense of what we're being tested on, it quickly becomes clear that this is one of those rare *Source/Audience* questions.

There aren't that many of these overall, but they tend to test two things:

1. is this person a practicing member of some profession, or just a random article-writer?

2. is this article intended for a knowledgeable audience, who might have some previous knowledge about any of its technical elements, or is it intended for a general audience that needs to have technical terms explained to them?

This passage seems to be speaking as a member of the legal profession. They are reading back the facts of the case, as though they're a law school professor teaching a case, or someone in a courtroom actively speaking about the case.

The final sentence of the 3rd paragraph provides our best clue as to who this voice belongs to:

"***this court** sees no reason to reject outright a form of evidence that has so ably withstood the test of time"*.

The voice is speaking for "this court". Only the judge gets to do that. So we can tell this was written by a judge.

choices.text: a judge presiding over an appeal of a criminal conviction
choices.explanation:
We can tell from the final sentence of the 3rd paragraph that this passage was written by a judge ("**this court** sees no reason to reject a form of evidence that has so ably withstood the test of time").

That's actually a good enough reason to pick this answer, since it's the only answer that says that the author is a judge.

But the final sentence of the passage suggests that we're at the Appellate (i.e. appeals) level, because this judge is reviewing the trial (lower) court's decision and vindicating it:

*The trial court below was therefore within its discretion in crediting testimony that ... [blah blah blah]*

choices.text: a defense attorney arguing an appeal of a client's criminal conviction
choices.explanation:
We're looking for judge, not attorney. An attorney can speak *about* "this court", but not *for* "this court".

An attorney could say, "This court found in *Marbury v. Madison* that a plaintiff's right to [blah blah blah]".

But only a judge can speak *as* the court, like we see at the end of the 3rd paragraph, "This court sees no reason to reject the fingerprinting evidence".

choices.text: a prosecutor arguing for the affirmation of a guilty verdict
choices.explanation:
We're looking for judge, not prosecutor. A prosecutor can speak *about* "this court", but not *for* "this court".

A prosecutor could say, "And thus we ask this court to find the defendant guilty."

But only a judge can speak *as* the court, like we see at the end of the 3rd paragraph, "This court sees no reason to reject the fingerprinting evidence".

choices.text: a professor of law lecturing to a criminal law class
choices.explanation:
We're looking for judge, not professor. A professor can speak *about* "this court", but not *for* "this court".

A professor could say, "This court found in *Simpson v. Springfield* that a plaintiff's right to [blah blah blah]".

But only a judge can speak *as* the court, like we see at the end of the 3rd paragraph, "This court sees no reason to reject the fingerprinting evidence".

choices.text: an academic presenting a paper to a group of legal scholars
choices.explanation:
We're looking for judge, not academic. An academic can speak *about* "this court", but not *for* "this court".

An academic could say, "This court found in *Simpson v. Springfield* that a plaintiff's right to [blah blah blah]".

But only a judge can speak *as* the court, like we see at the end of the 3rd paragraph, "This court sees no reason to reject the fingerprinting evidence".

questions.prompt: Each passage discusses the relationship between the reliability of the practice of fingerprint identification and which one of the following?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Both passages had moments where they were impugning the reliability of fingerprint identification.

In Passage A, these are mostly clustered in the 2nd paragraph.
In Passage B, the 1st paragraph.

We can actually find a few points of overlap. Both of those areas mention:
- no established error rates
- a lack of uniform, objective standards
- no standard for number of "points of identification" to call something a match

The answer might be something else, so we should stay flexible. And if we have access to CTRL/CMND + F, we might want to take keywords from an answer and search for them, to see if they appear in both passages.

choices.text: the ability of a criminal defendant to expose weaknesses in the prosecution's case
choices.explanation:
Only Passage A even uses the word "defendant". It never explicitly talks about any relationship between the defendant's ability to expose weakness in the case against them and fingerprinting reliability. We can implicitly tell that the defendant *did* try to argue that the fingerprinting evidence used against them exposes a weakness in the case against them, because, they argue, that fingerprinting is not established to be reliable.

That does not qualify as "the passage **discusses**", but luckily we don't have to devote any thought to this. After all, the word/idea of a 'defendant' doesn't come up in Passage B at all.

choices.text: the personal integrity of individual fingerprint examiners
choices.explanation: Neither passage brings up the personal integrity of fingerprint examiners (i.e. "fingerprinting isn't reliable because there are unscrupulous examiners who lie about their findings").

choices.text: differences in the identification practices used by various fingerprint examiners
choices.explanation:
This connects with 1 or 2 of the overlaps we found:

- no established error rates
**- a lack of uniform, objective standards**
**- no standard for number of "points of identification" to call something a match**

Since there aren't uniform, objective standards, there are differences. If things aren't uniform, then there are differences.

And if there's no accepted standard regarding the number of "points of identification" needed, then the identification practices of one examiner might be "if I see at least 10 matches, it's a match" whereas another might be "if I see at least 12 matches, it's a match".

choices.text: the partial or smudged prints that are typically used as evidence in criminal cases
choices.explanation: A quick search for "partial" or "smudged" will show us that this idea only shows up in Passage B.

choices.text: use of the holistic approach to fingerprint identification
choices.explanation:
A quick search for "holistic" will show us that this idea only shows up in Passage B.

Also, in B, the holistic assessment itself isn't discussed as a sign that fingerprint identification might be unreliable.

Rather, the *variability* of methods is what's discussed as a sign that fingerprint identification might be unreliable. The author is saying, "Some people do *point-counting*, some do holistic. Either way, there's no generally agreed-on standard."

questions.prompt: Which one of the following principles underlies the arguments in both passages?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
This is almost like doing an Agree question in LR -- the two parties fundamentally disagreed, so finding the common ground feels tricky.

Let's try to articulate what principle we think underlies the argument in each passage:

For Passage A, the implied conclusion is "fingerprinting is a respectable form of evidence", and some of the reasons given were "examiners are held to a consistent approach to identification / they're regularly subjected to testing / uniform standards have been established / it's been used for 100 years with experts concurring about its reliability".

So A's principle is kinda like,
*If a form of evidence is long-standing and those who gather the evidence are held to rigorous and consistent standards, it should be allowed in court*.

Passage B's conclusion is more like "fingerprinting is not a respectable form of evidence", and some of the reasons were "there aren't objective standards / no consensus / not a clear sense of the risk of false-positives / error rate hasn't been given much study".

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
Both parties talk about whether or not there are objective standards / whether or not examiners are tested for proficiency, and then connect that to whether or not fingerprinting evidence should be allowed in court or respected as a form of evidence.

So maybe the answer will have something to do with that? Tough to predict.

choices.text: Courts should be extremely reluctant to reject those forms of evidence that have withstood the test of time.
choices.explanation:
This matches a sentiment that Passage A had, but we can't match this to Passage B, which never talked about whether fingerprinting has / hasn't *withstood the test of time*.

B never argued, "since fingerprinting evidence hasn't withstood the test of time, we shouldn't be reluctant to reject it as a form of evidence" (that's also an illegal negation of what this answer says).

choices.text: Defendants should have the right to challenge forms of evidence whose reliability has not been scientifically proven.
choices.explanation: Neither argument is about defendants' procedural right to challenge evidence. A addresses whether the challenge warrants rejecting the evidence; B critiques the identification methods themselves. A principle permitting a challenge does not explain either evaluation of reliability.

choices.text: To evaluate the value of fingerprint evidence, one must know how likely it is that partial prints from two different people would match.
choices.explanation: B explicitly says these probabilities are critical to evaluating fingerprint evidence. A does not discuss partial prints or the probability of two such prints matching, so this principle does not underlie both arguments. Differing conclusions do not by themselves rule out a shared conditional principle; the issue is whether both arguments rely on it.

choices.text: Fingerprint identification should not be considered to have a low error rate unless rigorously conducted tests have shown this to be so.
choices.explanation:
This rule says,

*If rigorous testing has then fingerprinting*
*not shown fingerprinting → should not be*
*to have a low error rate considered to have*
*low error rate*

This is definitely something the author of B is talking about in her final paragraph, but does the author of A talk about this?

Not really. Passage A thinks that it was fine for the trial court to say that fingerprinting has a low error rate, but the rationale for that wasn't based on "rigorous tests having proven it".

choices.text: Fingerprint examiners must follow objective standards if fingerprint identification is to be reliable.
choices.explanation: Both authors treat objective standards as a requirement relevant to reliable identification. B stresses their absence to question reliability. A defends reliability by insisting that examiners follow a consistent approach and that professional training and peer review have established uniform standards. A's defense thus addresses the requirement rather than denying it. This does not mean that meeting a necessary condition alone proves reliability; A also invokes testing and the method's track record.

questions.prompt: Both passages allude to a method of fingerprint identification in which examiners

choices.text: rely on a holistic impression of how similar two fingerprints are
use computerized databases to search for matching fingerprints
count the number of characteristics two fingerprints have in common
calculate the odds of two different individuals' sharing certain very rare fingerprint characteristics
use computer technology to clarify the images of smudged or partial fingerprints

questions.prompt: Passage B differs from passage A in that passage B is more

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Since we're being asked for a difference between passage B and A, we should probably start with the most obvious difference -- Passage B seems pretty skeptical of the trustworthiness of fingerprint evidence, whereas Passage A is more confident and trustworthy that fingerprinting evidence is legit.

So passage B is more skeptical, inquiring, unsettled?

choices.text: optimistic in its conclusions
choices.explanation: Given that Passage B is more skeptical of whether we should be trusting fingerprinting evidence as much as we do, if anything we would say that Passage B is more *pessimistic*.

choices.text: general in focus
choices.explanation:
This doesn't have anything to do with each author's main stance towards fingerprinting, but if we ask ourselves, "*Did* Passage B have a more general focus than Passage A?", the answer is definitely 'yes'.

After all, Passage B's essay is about fingerprinting in general. How much can we trust it, given that it doesn't have uniform / standardized practices and given that we have very fuzzy estimations of its accuracy.

Passage A, although it does delve into some of these general questions, is at heart still written by an Appeals court judge, weighing in on the specific issue of whether the lower trial court was correct in admitting fingerprinting evidence of this specific defendant's trial.

choices.text: tentative in its claims
choices.tag: Fails B: Claims vs. Fingerprinting Attitude
choices.explanation:
B's author is more tentative when it comes to trusting fingerprinting evidence, but B's author isn't tentative in his claims.

Look at his first three sentences:
*- fingerprint examiners* *****lack***** *objective standards*
*- there is simply* *****no consensus*****
*- there is* *****no fixed requirement*****

As it continues, B's author says more stuff like
- ****no**** fingerprint examiner can answer such questions
- the answers are critical
- the error rate has received little study

Passage A definitely uses some non-tentative claims in its final paragraph, but since we can't point to any tentative claims in Passage B, we can't say that B was *more tentative*.

Passage B is uncertain about what the actual accuracy of fingerprinting is, but he's not tentative about claiming that uncertainty. He is definitively, passionately claiming that uncertainty.

choices.text: respectful of opposing claims
choices.explanation: A acknowledges possible differences among agencies and the desirability of further testing before defending the evidence. B does not show greater respect for opposing claims. The contrast is the general scope of B versus A's decision about a particular appeal, not an assumption that judges must use a respectful tone.

choices.text: dependent on unsubstantiated assumptions
choices.explanation: B identifies gaps in the evidentiary basis for trusting fingerprint identification: no agreed matching standard, unknown probabilities of resemblance, and little systematic study of errors. It does not become more dependent on unsubstantiated assumptions by identifying those gaps. In particular, B does not assign a probability to coincidental matches; its point is that the probability is unknown.

passages.title: Toni Morrison’s Jazz
passages.text:
Music and literature, rivals among the arts, have not coexisted without intruding on each other’s terrain. Ever since what we think of as “literature” developed out of the sounds of spoken, sung, and chanted art, writing has aspired to the condition of music, in which form contributes significantly to content. Nowhere is this truer than in the African American tradition, whose music is often considered its greatest artistic achievement and one of the greatest contributions to North American art. But while many African American writers have used musicians and music as theme and metaphor in their writing, none had attempted to draw upon a musical genre as the structuring principle for an entire novel until Toni Morrison did so in her 1992 novel *Jazz*, a novel set in the Harlem section of New York City in 1926.

In *Jazz*, the connection to music is found not only in the novel’s plot but, more strikingly, in the way in which the story is told. The narration slips easily from the third-person omniscience of the narrator’s disembodied voice—which, though sensitive and sympathetic, claims no particular identity, gender, or immersion in specific social circumstances—to the first-person lyricism of key characters. But throughout these shifts, the narrator is both generous with the characters’ voices and protective of his or her mastery over the narrative as a whole. On the one hand, the central characters are given the responsibility of relating their parts of the overarching story, but on the other hand, their sections are set off by quotation marks, reminders that the narrator is allowing them to speak. In this way, the narrative is analogous in structure to the playing of a jazz band which intertwines its ensemble sound with the individuality of embedded solo performances.

In jazz, composer and conductor Duke Ellington was the first to construct his compositions with his individual musicians and their unique “voices” in mind. Yet no matter how lengthy his musicians’ improvisations, no matter how bold or inventive their solos might be, they always performed within the undeniable logic of the composer’s frame—they always, in other words, performed as if with quotation marks around their improvisations and solos. It is this same effect that Toni Morrison has achieved in *Jazz*, a literary rendering of an art of composition that Duke Ellington perfected around the time in which *Jazz* is set.

In this novel, Morrison has found a way, paradoxically, to create the sense of an ensemble of characters improvising within the fixed scope of a carefully constructed collective narration. By simulating the style of a genius of music while exhibiting Morrison’s own linguistic virtuosity, *Jazz* serves to redefine the very possibilities of narrative point of view.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The musical structure and narrative innovation of Toni Morrison's novel *Jazz*, especially how it draws from jazz music to shape its literary form.

**Framework**

Theme / Example

**Main Point**

Morrison’s *Jazz* stands out as the first African American novel to use a musical genre—jazz—as its structuring principle, not just thematically but in the very way the story is told, thus redefining what narrative point of view can do in literature. **(Best encapsulated in the final paragraph and in the sentences: "In this novel, Morrison has found a way, paradoxically, to create the sense of an ensemble of characters improvising within the fixed scope of a carefully constructed collective narration.")**

**P1: Literature inspired by music—Morrison’s innovation**

We’re told that music and literature have always influenced one another, especially in the African American tradition, but that Toni Morrison was the first to structure an entire novel based on a musical genre—jazz—with her 1992 novel *Jazz*.

**P2: How *Jazz* mimics jazz music in its narrative**

The passage explains that the novel doesn’t just reference music in its plot but replicates jazz’s structure in its narration. The storytelling shifts from a detached narrator to deeply personal voices of the characters, much like solos in a jazz band, with the narrator still controlling the overall “composition.”

**P3: Comparison to Duke Ellington’s musical innovations**

This paragraph brings in Duke Ellington’s composing style—writing pieces tailored to his musicians, encouraging individuality but always within the larger work. Morrison’s storytelling is compared to this, with her allowing character “solos” within her own carefully designed narrative frame.

**P4: Morrison’s narrative achievement and its significance**

The last paragraph sums up Morrison’s achievement: she manages to evoke jazz’s musical improvisation in her writing, redefining what’s possible for narrative point of view by combining linguistic artistry with musical structure.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately states the main point of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
We want to combine the *Central Topic* with the *Author's Purpose* in writing about that topic.

The central topic was the novel *Jazz*. How do we know? It was the only concept that was present in all four paragraphs.

Why was the author writing about this novel? What framework did we use?

This seemed like a *Highlight Noteworthy* passage, so the author's big one-sentence takeaway should be whatever she thought was most important / distinctive / or worth knowing about this novel.

The last sentence of the first paragraph (the most common place to find a Main Point sentence) seems to stress what the author finds most interesting:

*while many writers used musicians and music as theme and metaphor,* *****none***** *had attempted to draw upon a musical genre as the structuring principle until Toni Morrison's "Jazz".*

The 2nd paragraph expands on this: *the book's connection to music is found* *****more strikingly***** *in the way in which the story is told* (i.e. using principles of jazz as the structuring style for how the story is told).

The 3rd paragraph zooms in specifically on Duke Ellington's style of jazz, and says that "it is this same effect that Toni Morrison has achieved - *a literary rendering* of Ellington's art of composition.

The final paragraph wraps up this sentiment -- "In her novel, Morrison finds a way to create the sense of an ensemble of characters improvising within the fixed scope of a carefully constructed collective narration" (i.e. the way the book is structured / told is like jazz!)

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for something like, "*Jazz* was a noteworthy book because it was the first time someone used a musical genre's style as the structuring principle for a novel / a literary rendering of a musical style."

choices.text: In *Jazz* , Morrison has realized a significant artistic achievement in creating the first African American work of fiction whose plot, themes, and setting are all drawn from the world of jazz.
choices.explanation:
This answer would be great if we replaced "plot / themes / setting" with "structuring principle".

As the author says at the end of the first paragraph, "many other African American artists had used musicians and music as theme and metaphor in their writing", so Toni wasn't the first to do that.

choices.text: Morrison's striking description of a musical ensemble performance containing solo improvisations constitutes an important artistic innovation and makes *Jazz* an important model for other writers.
choices.explanation:
Just like (A), this is making it sound like Morrison's innovation was to write a book *about* jazz. It's claiming that her artistic innovation was to ****describe**** a musical ensemble performance containing solo improvisations.

The main point of the passage was that Morrison's innovation was that she wrote a book that *felt like* a musical ensemble performance containing solo improvisations.

Although this book happens to also be about the world of jazz, the "structuring principle" has nothing to do with the content of the book. It's all about the *way* the story was told .. a narrator (i.e. bandleader) creating the overall structure with sectioned-off quotations from difference characters (i.e. individual members of the ensemble getting their turn to take a solo).

The book could have been about the stock market and still had this jazz-like structuring principle that made it feel like an ensemble performance with solo improvs.

choices.text: Although many African American writers have used music as a central metaphor in their works, Morrison's 1992 novel is unique and innovative for using jazz as its central metaphor.
choices.explanation:
This goes back to the last sentence of the first paragraph again. Other in the past had used musicians and music as theme and metaphor in their writing.

But no one had ever made music ****the structuring principle**** of the novel.

The distinction wasn't, "other people had previously written non-jazz music books, but this was the first jazz music book".

The distinction was, "other people had previously written books that dealt with music, but this was the first book that used a musical genre as its stylistic form."

choices.text: Building on the works of many African American writers and musical composers, Morrison has over the years developed an innovative jazzlike style of narration, which she used especially effectively in the novel *Jazz* .
choices.tag: Out of Scope: over the years / Wrong Emphasis: not about Jazz
choices.explanation:
This answer relegates *Jazz* to the periphery. It shows up as an add-on modifier, but it's not discussed in the main clause. The main clause is that, "Over the years, Morrison developed an innovative jazzlike style of narration".

We have no idea if she used this jazzlike style of narration in any other books besides this one, so we can't support the idea that this "jazzlike style of narration" is her typical, signature style that permeates many years of writing.

This passage was about one specific book, *Jazz*, which was the ****first**** time that a book was based on a jazzlike style of storytelling: bandleader's 3rd person narration + key characters' 1st person quotation 'solos".

choices.text: In *Jazz* , Morrison has succeeded in creating an original and effective narrative strategy that is a literary analogue of Duke Ellington's style of musical composition.
choices.explanation:
This answer gives perhaps a surprising amount of spotlight to Duke Ellington, but saying that *Jazz* is a success because it employs "an original and effective ****narrative strategy****" is the best match we got from any answer choices for the fact that Morrison's book was original because it used jazz as a ****structuring principle**** for the novel.

What this narrative strategy a literary analogue of Ellington's musical style?

Yes! The end of the 3rd paragraph says that "It is this same effect [of Ellington's musical style] that Toni Morrison has achieved in *Jazz*, a ****literary rendering**** of an art of composition that Duke perfected."

questions.prompt: The author's discussion in the first paragraph proceeds in which one of the following ways?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The author *proceeds by* is the language we see in LR for question stems on ****Method**** of reasoning.

So we can activate a similar part of our brain for this. We want to try characterizing what the author is saying in abstract terms.

1. the author introduces a historical tension between two different art forms
2. the author applies this tension to African American art
3. the author zooms in on one specific artwork by an African American that blends these two forms in an unprecedented way.

choices.text: from a common claim about the arts, to a denial of this claim as applied to a particular artistic tradition, to a hypothesis about a particular individual
choices.explanation: The first ingredient is probably fine, but "denial" of this claim makes no sense, when the author transitions from the wide angle lens of Music vs. Literature into the medium field lens of African American art by saying "Nowhere is this ****truer**** than in the African American tradition".

choices.text: from a general remark about two art forms, to a similar observation about a particular artistic tradition, to a specific comment about a particular work that exemplifies the prior remarks
choices.explanation:
This matches our first two ingredients very well and the third ingredient reasonably well.

1. the author introduces a historical tension between two different art forms
*a general remark about two art forms*

2. the author applies this tension to African American art
*a similar observation about a particular artistic tradition*

3. the author zooms in on one specific artwork by an African American that blends these two forms in an unprecedented way.
*a particular work that exemplifies the prior remarks*

The fact that Toni Morrison's novel does something ****unprecedented**** makes it a tough match for "it ****exemplifies**** the prior stuff".

However, the prior remarks include "writing has aspired to the condition of music, in which form contributes significantly to content", and that's exactly what's happening in *Jazz*. Since Morrison is using a musical genre ****as a structuring principle****, the form is contributing to the content / the writing is aspiring to the condition of music.

Realistically, I would probably leave this but not pick it on a first pass and only come home to it because other answers are broken and we can better make this work.

choices.text: from a description of a common claim about two art forms, to some specific evidence that supports that claim, to an inference regarding a particular individual to whom that claim applies
choices.explanation:
The first ingredient seems okay?
1. the author introduces a historical tension between two different art forms
*a description of a common claim about two art forms*

Is there a common claim about literature and music? It's not saying that the two have something in common. It's saying they have always been rivals. I guess what they have in common is that they've always intruded on each other's terrain.

Does the author then provide specific evidence that supports that "music and literature have always intruded on each other's terrain"?

Not really. He says that literature has aspired to the condition of music, especially in the African American tradition. That's another weak match.

When we compare the 2nd ingredient of (B) to the 2nd ingredient here, it seems like (B)'s is an easier, more accurate match (a similar observation about a particular tradition).

Finally, does the author make an *inference* about a particular individual?

No, the author just describes an individual who wrote a book that involves literature and music swirling together. The author doesn't infer that Toni Morrison was an writer who intruded on music's terrain. He just says she wrote a book that had an innovative way of blending the two.

It feels like all 3 ingredients in this answer are stretchable if we had to, but we don't have to, because (B) provides easier to match language.

choices.text: from an observation about a specific art form, to a more general claim about the applicability of that observation to other art forms, to a particular counterexample to the first observation
choices.tag: Bad Match: specific art / more general
choices.explanation:
Does the first paragraph start with an observation about a specific art form? The first sentence is about two specific art forms.

We could ignore the first sentence and say that the author's 2nd sentence makes an observation about writing: "it has aspired to the condition of music".

Does the author go to a ****more general**** claim about the applicability of that to other art forms?

Definitely not. The claim was already about music, so there aren't any *other* art forms to apply that claim to. And the 2nd ingredient is getting more specific (not more general), about the music vs. literature tension within the African American tradition.

choices.text: from general comments about the arts, to a purported counterexample to the general comments as applied to a particular artistic tradition, to a description of a particular work that bears out the original comments
choices.explanation:
There is no general comments about "the arts", just one specifically about two arts, music and literature.

There is no counterexample. The author zooms into a particular artistic tradition (African American) by saying "nowhere is this truer than here". The first paragraph maintains the same theme and keeps zooming in two more layers of specificity.

questions.prompt: The author's assertion in the last sentence of the first paragraph would be most called into question if which one of the following were true?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
Lucky for us, this question stem just wants us to weaken an **assertion** (i.e. a claim), not an *argument*.

That means we don't really need to do anything besides read the claim that we're going to try to argue is not true.

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body:
The assertion has two prongs, so potentially we could fight either one of them, but it's more likely we would target the main clause.

Thus, we either want an answer that helps us say,
- No, or almost no, AA writers have ever used musicians and music as a theme or as a metaphor in their writing

or, more likely

- At least one AA writer prior to Morrison has attempted to draw upon a musical genre as the structuring principle for their novel

choices.text: Even a casual reading of *Jazz* makes it evident that the author has intentionally tried to simulate a style of jazz performance in the narration of the story.
choices.explanation:
This doesn't help us with either of our goals, since this answer is about *Jazz*, whereas our goals are about other AA writers, not Morrison.

GOAL 1: No, or almost no, AA writers have ever used musicians and music as a theme or as a metaphor in their writing

GOAL 2: At least one AA writer prior to Morrison has attempted to draw upon a musical genre as the structuring principle for their novel

choices.text: A small number of African American novelists writing earlier in the twentieth century sought to base the form of their work on the typical structure of blues music.
choices.explanation:
This helps us with Goal 2.

GOAL 2: At least one AA writer prior to Morrison has attempted to draw upon a musical genre as the structuring principle for their novel

It says that there were some AA writers prior to Morrison (**earlier** in the 20th century) who based the form (i.e. structuring principle) of their novels on the musical genre of blues.

choices.text: All novels about nonliterary arts and artists appear as if their authors have tried to make their narrative styles reminiscent of the arts in question.
choices.explanation:
This almost resembles a way to argue for our 2nd goal:

GOAL 2: At least one AA writer prior to Morrison has attempted to draw upon a musical genre as the structuring principle for their novel

But this answer isn't talking about any writers who used a musical genre as their *structuring principle*.

It's talking about writers who used some nonliterary art form (not necessarily music) to inform the narrative style (not structuring principle) of their novel.

It's not hopeless, but it's not as concretely relevant to the claim we're trying to undermine as (B) is.

choices.text: Depending partly on whether or not it is read aloud, any novel can be found to be somewhat musical in nature.
choices.explanation: The idea that a book, read aloud, could be "somewhat musical" in nature is miles away from proving what we're trying to say which is that, "Some writer, prior to Morrison, picked a specific genre of music to use as the structuring principle for their novel".

choices.text: A smaller number of African American writers than of non-African American writers in North America have written novels whose plots and characters have to do with music.
choices.tag: Irrelevant Comparison: AA vs. non-AA writers
choices.explanation:
The claim we're trying to undermine is exclusively about AA writers, so comparing AA writers to non-AA writers is totally beside the point.

And having a plot or character that has to do with music is not clearly the same as "I picked a genre of music as the structuring principle for my novel".

Finally, there's no time element to this answer, so even if it established that these AA writers had based the structure on their novel on a genre of music, we still wouldn't be able to say that this novel predated Morrison's, and thus we still wouldn't be undermining the passage's claim.

questions.prompt: The information in the passage most supports which one of the following statements regarding Ellington?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
All our info on Ellington comes in the 3rd paragraph, so this would be a *Semi-Defined Target*, meaning some people would find it worthwhile to re-read the 3rd paragraph before heading to the answers.

Others will feel strong enough about their gut understanding of Ellington's role in the passage to proceed to the answers.

A scan of the 3rd paragraph reminds us of several things we learned about Duke:
- he was the first to try to incorporate the unique voices of the individual musicians in his band into his compositions

- the individual musicians would take sometimes lengthy solos, but they would still be constrained by the "master logic" of Ellington's composition.

- Morrison tried to capture something similar with how she wrote *Jazz*

choices.text: Morrison has explicitly credited him with inspiring the style of narration that she developed in *Jazz* .
choices.explanation:
Nothing in the passage allows us to say that Morrison ever **explicitly** credited Ellington with inspiring the style of narration in *Jazz*.

The author definitely thinks that Morrison achieved a literary rendering of Ellington's style, but that doesn't mean Morrison was setting out to do so or ever explicitly credited Ellington with being the inspiration.

choices.text: He prevented his musicians from performing lengthy solos in order to preserve the unity of his compositions.
choices.explanation: Paragraph 3 expressly allows lengthy improvisations and bold, inventive solos within the composer's frame. Maintaining that frame therefore did not require preventing lengthy solos, as this choice claims.

choices.text: He is a minor character in Morrison's *Jazz* .
choices.explanation: Nothing in the passage suggests that Duke Ellington is a character in *Jazz*.

choices.text: He composed music that was originally intended to be performed by the specific musicians he conducted.
choices.explanation:
This matches nicely with the first sentence of the 3rd paragraph (and provides a good illustration of why it can be very useful to go back to the passage before checking out answers).

*Duke Ellington was the first to construct his compositions with his individual musicians and their unique "voices" in mind*.

This suggests that the music Ellington composed in such a way was intended to be played with his specific bandmates.

It would be silly for Ellington to compose a piece of music with the unique voices of his band members in mind (e.g. "Eddie can play this part; Felix will fit in here" etc.), if he weren't planning to play that piece with those band members.

choices.text: Though he composed and conducted primarily jazz, he also composed some music of other genres.
choices.explanation: Nothing in the 3rd paragraph indicates that Ellington worked in any styles besides jazz.

questions.prompt: The author's primary purpose in the passage is to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Our framework for this passage was *Highlight Noteworthy*, because the author is profiling a certain artistic work in order to highlight how it is distinctive and special.

Its specialness is revealed in the final sentence of the first paragraph, where the author says "it's the first novel that ever attempted to use a musical genre as the structuring principle".

So let's look for an answer that's like
- highlight why a certain novel was so innovative
- show how an author broke new ground with a certain work

choices.text: analyze and commend the variety of contributions to the art of the novel made by a particular writer
choices.explanation: This passage is all about ****one**** specific contribution made by Morrison in *Jazz* -- she told the story the way a jazz ensemble would perform a piece (the central thrust controlled by the bandleader / narrator, with first-person performances set off by quotations, like individual members of the ensemble taking a solo).

choices.text: contrast a particular African American writer's work with the work of African American practitioners of another art
choices.explanation:
This is saying that the author wanted to contrast Morrison's *novel* with work of African American artists from a different medium.

The only other artistic medium mentioned would be music. Was the author's purpose to contrast Morrison's *Jazz* with the musical work of Duke Ellington?

No, the opposite! The author was saying, "How cool is this writer's work! She managed to do a literary rendering of what Duke Ellington was doing with a different art form, jazz music."

choices.text: describe a particular aspect of one work by a particular writer
choices.explanation:
This aligns nicely with our Most Valuable Sentence, the final sentence of the first paragraph. The author wanted to *Highlight Something Noteworthy* about one particular work, the book *Jazz* by Toni Morrison.

What particular aspect did the author think was so noteworthy?
*No writer had attempted to* *****draw upon a musical genre as the structuring principle***** *for an entire novel until Toni Morrison did so in her 1992 novel 'Jazz'*.

choices.text: demonstrate the ways in which two apparently dissimilar arts are, on a deeper analysis, actually quite similar
choices.explanation:
The author isn't trying to make a broad case that even though literature and music seem like dissimilar arts, on deeper analysis they're actually quite similar.

This passage is specifically about the book *Jazz*. It's not about literature more broadly.

choices.text: detail the thematic concerns in the work of a particular writer and identify the sources of those concerns
choices.explanation:
In that most valuable sentence at the end of the 1st paragraph, the author actually specifically says that *Jazz* is not noteworthy for dealing with music as theme / metaphor (after all many African American writers had already done that).

It's interesting because *the way the story was told*, the structure of the book, was a literary version of Duke Ellington's signature style of ensemble jazz.

questions.prompt: Each of the following excerpts from the passage exhibits the author's attitude toward the novel *Jazz* EXCEPT:

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: There's no reason to try to do any pre-gaming here. We have five specific line references to consider, and with each one we just have to ask ourselves, "Is this line expressing the author's attitude about the book *Jazz*?"

choices.text: "...whose music is often considered its greatest artistic achievement and one of the greatest contributions to North American art" (first paragraph)
choices.explanation:
This sentence is not talking about the book *Jazz*. In fact, the book hasn't even been brought up yet in the passage.

Thus, there's no way this sentence is showing the author's attitude toward *Jazz*.

choices.text: "In *Jazz* , the connection to music is found not only in the novel's plot but, more strikingly, in the way in which the story is told" (second paragraph)
choices.explanation:
This shows part of the author's attitude about the book *Jazz*.

Specifically, the author finds it **striking** that the way the book is told itself resembles jazz.

choices.text: "The narration slips easily from the third-person omniscience of the narrator's disembodied voice..." (second paragraph)
choices.explanation:
This shows part of the author's attitude about the book *Jazz*.

Specifically, the author finds the transitions between a 3rd person omniscient narrator and 1st person narrators to be impressively smooth.

It slips **easily** from one narrator's voice into another's.

choices.text: "...Morrison has found a way, paradoxically, to create the sense of an ensemble of characters improvising within the fixed scope..." (fourth paragraph)
choices.explanation: The author admires Morrison's ability to combine the impression of individual improvisation with a carefully constructed overall narration. The paradox concerns freedom within a fixed structure; it does not require treating improvisation as sloppy or disorganized.
